messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Re: Small error in spec function (and proposed fix)
messages.subject_clean: [seewave] Re: Small error in spec function (and proposed fix)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dan,
Thank you very much for noting this issue.
It is true that I always thought about even signals.
I will fix this in the next version of seewave.
Best
Jerome

De: "Dan Ridley-Ellis" <d.ridl...@napier.ac.uk>
À: "seewave GROUP" <see...@googlegroups.com>
Envoyé: Vendredi 24 Novembre 2017 00:46:17
Objet: [seewave] Re: Small error in spec function (and proposed fix)

I confirmed there is a problem. The attached example is the result of 2000 mathematically generated damped sine waves. Analysis is over a 2 second period at 44.1 kHz sampling rate - which means an odd number of points. Frequency accuracy error is biased by half an fft bin at the top end - and this is the result of an error in how the x vector is calculated within spec.

Script along these lines works

        x = seq(0, (f/2), length.out = length(y) + 1)/1000
        x = head(x, n = length(x)-1)

where y is the vector of of FFT amplitudes, already cut in half from what comes out of fft()

Dan

On Tuesday, 21 November 2017 00:01:03 UTC, Dan Ridley-Ellis wrote:
>
> Hi
> I've been throwing a bunch of mathematically generated waves at the spec function and I've noticed that it makes a small error when the wave has an odd number of points in the time domain.   I think this caused by the way that the vector of frequency bins is calculated in the spec function.
>
>
> The error means that frequencies at the high end are, on average, in error by half the width of a fft frequency bin when there an odd number of points in the time domain.
>
> If there an even number of points, no problems
>
>
>
> In the spec function there is the code for the frequency bins x:
>
>
>  if (is.null(at)) {
>
>           x <- seq(0, (f/2) - (f/n), length.out = n%/%2)/1000
>
>         }
>
>         else {
>
>           x <- seq(0, (f/2) - (f/wl), length.out = n%/%2)/1000
>
>         }
>
>
>
> This seems to work better (but I am not sure why)
>
>
>   if (is.null(at)) {
>
>           x <- seq(0, (f/2) - (f/n) - n%%2, length.out = n%/%2)/1000
>
>         }
>
>         else {
>
>           x <- seq(0, (f/2) - (f/wl) - n%%2, length.out = n%/%2)/1000
>
>         }
>
>
>
> Dan

--

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] ffilter small frequency ranges
messages.body_plain:
Dear Irene

The function ffilter() works on the FFT which is parametrized with the argument wl.
When you have a sound sampled at f=44100 and that you set wl=512 then the frequency resolution of the FFT is \Delta_{f} = 44100/512 = 86.13 Hz which is above or very close to the frequency bandpass you set (between 10 Hz or 100 Hz). The filter cannot work properly then.

Try the function fir() instead. It should better work.

HTH

Jerome

De: "Irene Roca" <irene.torr...@gmail.com>
À: "seewave GROUP" <see...@googlegroups.com>
Envoyé: Lundi 20 Novembre 2017 17:40:56
Objet: [seewave] ffilter small frequency ranges

Hello all,

I'm using the function ffilter from seewave to filter out small frequency bands (10 Hz or 100Hz) from a sound signal (44.1kHz, 16bit) and I observed that for frequency bands smaller than 150Hz, there is a particular pattern that appears in the frequency spectrum that I can't explain. Sistematically, each x frequency bands, there is one band with lower amplitude than the rest and then the amplitude of the next band rises again (see figure 1). I appears as two signals instead of one. It does not happens when the frequency bands are bigger than 150Hz. You can see both spectrums in the files attached. Does anybody knows what is caussing this pattern?

I let you here the code I used to produce the figures:

a <- readWave(file=file.choose(),header=FALSE)

Figure 1:
ffa <- ffilter(a, from = 1000, to = 1050, bandpass = TRUE, wl=512, ovlp=50,  output="Wave")
b <- spectro(ffa,wl=512, ovlp=50, plot = FALSE, norm=FALSE)
amplitude <- apply(b$amp, 1, mean)
plot(b$freq,amplitude)

Figure 2:
ffa <- ffilter(a, from = 1000, to = 2000, bandpass = TRUE, wl=512, ovlp=50,  output="Wave")
b <- spectro(ffa,wl=512, ovlp=50, plot = FALSE, norm=FALSE)
amplitude <- apply(b$amp, 1, mean)
plot(b$freq,amplitude)

Thank you very much for your help
Best wishes

--

messages.subject: window length argument not passed to sspectro in ACI code.
messages.subject_clean: window length argument not passed to sspectro in ACI code.
messages.body_plain:
Developers,

In doing some testing of our in house codes against Seewave, I've notice that the window length (wl) argument is not passed on to sspectro in the ACI routine.

z <- sspectro <https://rdrr.io/cran/seewave/man/seewave.internal.html>(wave, f, wn=wn, ovlp=ovlp)

Therefore (if I'm interpreting the code correctly?) NFFT will default to 512 in all calculations, and if the frequency limits are used the wrong rows will be selected from the spectrogram matrix.

regards,
-del

Dear Del,

You are absolutely right. Sorry for this bug that will be fixed in the next version of seewave, that should be released soon if CRAN team let it pass...

If needed just replace:

z <- sspectro(wave, f, wn=wn, ovlp=ovlp)

by
z <- sspectro(wave, f, wl = wl, wn = wn, ovlp = ovlp)

Thank you,

Jerome

Developers,

In doing some testing of our in house codes against Seewave, I've notice that the window length (wl) argument is not passed on to sspectro in the ACI routine.

z <- sspectro <https://rdrr.io/cran/seewave/man/seewave.internal.html>(wave, f, wn=wn, ovlp=ovlp)

Therefore (if I'm interpreting the code correctly?) NFFT will default to 512 in all calculations, and if the frequency limits are used the wrong rows will be selected from the spectrogram matrix.

regards,
-del
